title: HTTP: corrected memory management and tracking for header_value_map
description:
As [pointed out](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20795#note_2710277919) by @johnthacker, header_value_map in updated HTTP dissector eats up memory on each pass of non-streamed HTTP.
This MR corrects memory management and tracking/storage of the headers.

Thanks for looking at this. I think this works. Eventually it might be possible to simplify the code a bit (e.g., `tail_prv_data` is retrieved several times, and it's probably possible to avoid storing the `header_value_map` in different places for the streaming chunk handling now that you're storing it for all requests and responses, and some of the checking for an existing map may be able to happen earlier.)

It still means that now there's extra memory use for all HTTP in order to persistently store the headers even though only some HTTP uses (largely Upgrade) need it, but at least it's not allocating every pass.

In the case where there's Upgrade it doesn't matter too much that all the headers are stored in persistent memory, but when there are many ordinary requests and responses as part of a HTTP session the effect of the previous commit still means faster growing memory use on, e.g., a long running TShark process, for headers that don't actually need to be saved. (It might be too complicated to only copy the map to file scoped memory if an Upgrade or similar header is found, I suppose.)

Could catch. Submitted https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/21218 to address this

So this approach doesn't work, because this is all inside the `while (tvb_offset_exists(tvb, offset)) {` loop back at line 1624 or so.

In some cases (due to fuzzing or whatever) it seems that the `header_value_map` is allocated with `pinfo->pool` but (because of a later line that does look like a request or reply, perhaps) it ends up getting stored in the `wmem_file_scope()` conversation data and then retrieved in a later frame once it has already been freed.

A summary of the issue:

1. Originally, the HTTP dissector would stop to reassembly bodies completely based on Content-Length. Since the payload was not handed to the next dissector until that happened, the headers were only scoped to have a lifetime of the frame (in which reassembly occurred.)
2. Some (e.g. gRPC, I believe) protocols use HTTP chunked transfer encoding as a persistent HTTP connection and stream independent chunks that preferably should be dissected as they come in. Some dissectors want access to the headers each time they access a chunk, which means that the headers have to be saved in persistent file scoped memory from the frame that contains them so that they can be passed to each frame with a chunk.
3. Other protocols use HTTP Upgrade, where subsequent frames don't have any HTTP framing, but some of those dissectors still want access to the headers from the last HTTP request and response that contained the Upgrade header and switched to the other protocol in each subsequent frame, because it provides state information for how the other dissector should operate. (Alternatively, those dissectors could save the state information themselves very first time they are called, but they don't do that right now, they rely on the HTTP dissector doing that. The alternative solution would have the advantage of only saving the headers useful for the dissector, instead of all headers - previously the HTTP dissector saved only the Websocket-relevant headers, but that was removed as requiring the HTTP dissector to know too much about Websocket and possibly other dissectors.)
4. As part of the recent changes, the headers are saved in persistent memory any time a request and response is seen (even though not all follow on dissectors need the headers in subsequent frames, since most do not operate in a streaming mode.) We might only need to do that if we see an Upgrade header, though I suppose the current approach might have been simpler in some ways.
5. We don't really know if we need file scoped memory instead of pinfo->pool scoped memory until the headers are completely parsed, but the process of parsing the headers puts them inside the header value map. One approach, possibly, would be to insert the headers into a pinfo->pool scoped map initially and then copy it at the end to file scoped memory if it turns out to be necessary. Another approach would be freeing the map at the end if it turns out not to be necessary to store it. (Note that freeing a wmem map does not necessarily free its keys and values, which have to be freed manually.) Another approach would be to just increase the memory usage.

The key problem with `pinfo->pool` approach is that the headers could be split across multiple packets. To make matters slightly more complex, in HTTP/1 upgrade protocol is defined in the response since client can offer multiple upgrade protocols.
In the next few days I'll work on MR to implement the freeing approach - I think this is the most universal option.

> The key problem with pinfo->pool approach is that the headers could be split across multiple packets.

That is true, though the typical behavior when there isn't a empty line with only a CRLF (see where `req_resp_hdrs_do_reassembly()` is called) is to tell the TCP dissector to reassemble additional segments and only dissect when the headers are reassembled. (That preference can be turned off, and also reassembly doesn't happen if, e.g., TCP checksum checking is enabled and the checksum is bad.)

Websocket only needs to parse the HTTP Sec-Websocket- headers once, not every time it is called. It should be Websocket's responsibility to save the information from just the headers it needs into its own file scoped memory, rather than having the HTTP dissector store everything in file scoped memory. That's probably true for other Upgrade protocols. I think probably I would alter this and f82ed9a537379aeb29a7cd1dbe3b9e024c97ecd8.

If `header_value_map` is *not* NULL here, but was allocated on a previous line pinfo->pool scoped (because of odd or fuzzed or otherwise buggy data where a request or reply line occurred after something that looked like a header line) then the `pinfo->pool` scoped map is now being stored inside `prv_data`, and will be retrieved later after it's expired.
